newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: OPINION - RBNZ unlikely to ease before January.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - RBNZ unlikely to ease before January.

text.p: By Jason Wong, Economist First NZ Capital.
WELLINGTON, Sept 5 - Next week the Reserve Bank of New Zealand gives its assessment of the state of the economy with the release of its Economic Projections.
The policy message is expected to be similar to that of its June Monetary Policy Statement (MPS) -- the time has not yet arrived for an easing in monetary conditions.
Imagine yourself in Dr Brash's shoes. Your mandated inflation target is 0-2 percent, yet underlying inflation stands at 2.3 percent in the year to June.
Forecasts show annual underlying inflation rising to around 2.7 percent in September, and remaining above 2.0 percent until June 1997.
You have a strong hunch that inflation in 12-18 months will be around an annualised 1.0 percent, but you thought the same thing this time last year and you were wrong.
Are you going to ease?
We say "no".
Monetary policy remains very tight, but there has been no convincing evidence over the quarter which is likely to change the bank's stance.
Recent data on activity has been mixed. A mixture of data is what one would expect around a turning point in the economy. On the weak side:
- the most recent GDP data showed annualised growth of only 1.6 percent in the March quarter.
- retail sales growth looks relatively subdued in the face of strong rises in household incomes.
- business confidence is relatively low, although it has just moved back into positive territory after almost reaching recession-warning levels.
- dwelling consents have plummeted over the last three months and confidence in the residential building sector is pessimistic.
However, other data suggests that the economy is not in as bad a shape as the above indicators suggest:
- money and credit aggregates are still growing very strongly.
- employment growth continues to surprise on the upside.
- consents for factories and industrial buildings rose nearly 65 percent in the six months to June.
- imports of capital plant have accelerated over the last few months to reach 11.1 percent year-on-year.
On inflation, the June quarter Consumer Price Index was higher than expected, with inflation in the housing market continuing to surprise on the upside.

Real Estate Institute of New Zealand (REINZ) data for July showed house prices 5.0 percent below their peak in March, but the quality-adjusted Valuation New Zealand data showed a provisional rise of an annualised 7.0 percent in the June quarter (in a rising market, provisional figures get revised upward).

The Labour Cost Index showed wage growth at a surprisingly low 0.3 percent in the June quarter, but a survey of contracts by the Department of Labour showed the opposite trend -- one of a continued acceleration in wage growth.

The Producer Price Index (PPI) fell in the June quarter, but the movement was largely driven by commodity price falls. In any case, the PPIs have already been well behaved for some time now. The important point is that new data over the last quarter has provided us with little confidence of a significant reduction in non-tradeables inflation -- the sector of greatest concern to the bank.
While the real economy may be progressing as sluggishly as expected, the bank does not have the confidence on falling inflation pressures that it needs to ease monetary policy.
So when will the bank ease?
The quarterly average of our monetary conditions indicator -- based on the Trade-Weighted Index and 90-day rates -- has a 90 percent-plus correlation with annual underlying inflation.
In spite of monetary policy in principle being directed by inflation 12-18 months ahead, monetary policy is overwhelmingly influenced by current inflation pressures.
An easing will take place once good underlying inflation figures are realised.
The September quarter CPI is not likely to be the catalyst, as a quarterly underlying inflation result around 0.5-0.6 percent is expected.
The immediate pre and post-election period could also result in financial market instability -- not a good time to be easing monetary policy.
The December quarter CPI due mid-January appears to be the earliest time a formal easing could take place.
However, in anticipation of a good outcome, financial markets would lead short rates lower towards the end of 1996.
Talk of a possible near-term easing by the bank in its December Monetary Policy Statement could also be a notable signpost.
However, in addition to good underlying inflation figures, the bank needs some clear evidence that wage inflation has peaked.
As wages explain 70 percent of consumer prices, the bank cannot afford to be too complacent on labour market pressures.
A third requirement for an easing in monetary policy is a well-behaved housing market. It would be premature to get too excited about recent housing market developments.

The REINZ may have shown recent weakness in house prices and activity, but the more respected Valuation New Zealand figures still show house price inflation at levels indicative of a demand and supply imbalance.
(Note - The opinions expressed in this article represent the views of the author only. They should not be seen as reflecting the views of Reuters)
